title: Speed-time / velocity-time graph problem
what_it_asks: You are given a piecewise-linear speed-time graph, or a description of motion you must turn into one. You find accelerations, distances and sometimes an unknown speed or time. The idea is that the gradient gives acceleration and the area under the graph gives distance.
typical_structure: Usually three parts, sometimes two or four. Early parts are short, often a sketch or a single acceleration worth two or three marks. Later parts are longer, such as a distance or an unknown speed, worth four or more marks. Later parts often reuse a value from an earlier part or from your sketch, and a show-that part sometimes appears. About a quarter of the questions come with a printed diagram.
mark_pattern: Sketch parts are mostly independent marks, typically B1 B1 or B1 B1 B1, for the correct shape, the labelled key values and the final segment. Short calculation parts are usually M1 A1: a method mark for a gradient, a suvat formula or an area, then an accuracy mark for the value. Longer parts run M1 A1 A1 or M1 A1 M1 A1 A1. There you form an area or an equation in the unknown, then solve it. Sometimes the pattern is M1 A1 dM1 A1, where the dM1 is the solving step and depends on the first M1. An A1ft can be earned when you correctly use a value from an earlier part. A show-that part ends with A1*, which needs a complete, error-free argument.

where_marks_leak.text: Many students give the final answer to the wrong number of significant figures or decimal places. The final A1 is lost even though the method was right.
You round a speed or time part-way through, then use it in an area or an equation. The final answer drifts outside what is accepted, so the A1 goes, and so can a later A1ft.
You find the area when the question wants acceleration, or use the gradient when it wants distance. The M1 is lost, and the A1 and any dM1 that depend on it go too.
If the graph goes below the axis, you give displacement when distance was asked, or the reverse. The method may earn the M1 but the A1 is lost.
A slip in a trapezium area or a division gives a wrong value from a correct method. The A1 is lost, though the M1 stays.

write_to_earn: Write the method line first, such as gradient = change in speed over time, or area = half the sum of the parallel sides times the width, before you substitute.
On a sketch, label every key speed and time on the axes and mark the end of each straight segment, since each label can earn its own B1.
Split the area into trapezia or rectangles and triangles, and show each piece, so the M1 is secure even if one piece is wrong.
When the speed is unknown, put it in as a letter, form the equation from the total area or gradient, and solve it in a separate visible step.
In a show-that part, write the line just before the printed result, then the result, and reject any invalid root with a reason.
